::: {.callout-warning}
Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision. This module teaches the physics behind
electrical safety; it does not replace the safety standards, and its numbers are not design limits.
:::

## In 60 seconds

A mapping system puts electrodes inside the heart, so the electronics connect to the most sensitive organ through a
low-resistance path. Microamperes of mains-frequency current that would go unnoticed on the skin can capture the
ventricle when they enter through a catheter, because a small electrode concentrates current: the density at a
hemisphere of radius $a$ is $I/(2\pi a^2)$. In 40 patients, 60-Hz currents as low as 20 µA caused intermittent capture
and 49 µA caused fibrillation. Every isolation barrier leaks a capacitive current $2\pi f C V$, and leakages from
several devices on one patient can add, so isolation capacitance is a design budget. The front end must also survive
what the procedure itself delivers: a defibrillation pulse, handled by series resistors and clamps whose current is
$(V - V_c)/R$, and RF ablation energy at hundreds of kilohertz, which must be filtered before any nonlinearity turns
it into a baseband shift of $\beta A^2/2$.

## From the field

- **Silent capture.** In 40 patients studied during implantable cardioverter-defibrillator testing, 60-Hz current applied through a
  right-ventricular catheter caused intermittent capture from 20 µA, continuous capture from 32 µA and fibrillation from
  49 µA. Continuous capture collapsed the arterial pressure with no ECG sign of the current [@swerdlow1999].
- **The standard was at the edge.** That study noted a national single-fault limit of 50 µA and found continuous capture
  at or below it in 22% of patients with bipolar current [@swerdlow1999].
- **Fluid paths count.** In a bench test of dialysis blood lines run to the IEC 60601-1 procedure for cardiac-floating
  (CF) devices, leakage at a central catheter's tip exceeded the 50 µA CF limit in several test conditions
  [@jonsson2005].
- **Combinations create risk.** A review notes that combinations of separately approved equipment and connections can
  still put a patient at risk, and that more direct pathways to the heart make patients more vulnerable
  [@burgess2019].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $f$ mains frequency (Hz); $C$ isolation capacitance (F); $V$ rms voltage across it (V);
$I$ rms current (A); $I_{\lim}$ a current limit; $a$ electrode radius (m); $r$ distance from the electrode center; $A$
a body cross-section (m²); $J$ current density (A/m²); $V_{in}$ voltage reaching a protected input; $V_c$ clamp voltage;
$R$ series resistance; $T$ pulse duration; $V_b$, $R_b$ voltage across and resistance of the body during
defibrillation; $f_c$ filter corner; $n$ filter order; $A_{RF}$ RF amplitude at an input; $\beta$ second-order
nonlinearity coefficient (1/V).

### Leakage through isolation

An isolation barrier separates the patient circuit from mains-powered circuits, but its capacitance still passes a
current. Several devices on one patient, fed from the same mains, can add in phase:

$$
I = 2\pi f C V, \qquad I_{\text{total}} = \Bigl\lvert \sum_k I_k e^{j\phi_k} \Bigr\rvert \le \sum_k I_k, \qquad C_{\max} = \frac{I_{\lim}}{2\pi f V}
$$ {#eq-m15-leakage}

At 230 V and 50 Hz, 100 pF passes 7.2 µA; keeping one device under 20 µA allows 277 pF, and three equal devices
under 20 µA allow 92 pF each (lab part A). IEC 60601-1 classifies applied parts by how they contact the patient, with
the cardiac-floating (CF) type for direct cardiac connection [@jonsson2005]; its limits are what designs are tested
against, and this module does not restate them.

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m15-leakage with every device's leakage in phase (the worst case) and the patient grounded; reference
  lines at the minimum currents for intermittent capture and fibrillation reported by @swerdlow1999. Tested against
  `epml.safety`.
- Parameters: capacitance, device count, mains voltage and frequency are adjustable illustrative choices.
- What it ignores: resistive leakage, the measuring network a standard specifies, the patient's own impedance, other
  fault paths and phase differences between supplies.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Isolation capacitance sets leakage: budget it across every device on the patient.

### Microshock and current density

Current entering the heart through a small electrode spreads radially from it. Through a hemisphere of radius $r$ the
same current crosses an area $2\pi r^2$:

$$
J(r) = \frac{I}{2\pi r^2}, \qquad \frac{J(a)}{I/A} = \frac{A}{2\pi a^2}
$$ {#eq-m15-density}

Compared with the same current spread over a body cross-section $A$, a 1-mm electrode concentrates it about 8000-fold
for an illustrative $A$ of 0.05 m² (lab part B). This is why intracardiac connections face currents orders of
magnitude below those felt on the skin. The density also falls as $1/r^2$, so the tissue right at the electrode is the
tissue that is stimulated, as in pacing (m11).

**Key takeaways**

- A catheter turns a harmless current into a concentrated one.

### Defibrillation protection

During external defibrillation, part of the pulse appears across the recording electrodes. A common protection network
is a series resistor followed by a clamp. For a rectangular pulse of duration $T$:

$$
I = \frac{V_{in} - V_c}{R}, \qquad E_R = \frac{(V_{in} - V_c)^2\,T}{R}, \qquad \frac{V_{in} I}{V_b^2/R_b} \;\text{(share of the body's power taken by one input)}
$$ {#eq-m15-defib}

A larger $R$ lowers the current, the energy each part must absorb and the energy diverted from the heart, at the cost
of thermal noise (m14) and bandwidth with the input capacitance. With illustrative values (500 V at the input, a 10 V
clamp, a 10 ms pulse), a 10-kΩ resistor absorbs 0.24 J and diverts about 0.05% of the body's power (lab part C).
Pulsed field ablation (m28) raises the same questions with its own pulses.

### RF ablation energy

RF ablation runs at 300 kHz to 1 MHz [@berjano2006], and the RF voltage at the recording inputs can exceed the
microvolt signals by many orders of magnitude. A low-pass of order $n$ attenuates far above its corner by:

$$
\lvert H(f)\rvert = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^{2n}}} \approx \left(\frac{f_c}{f}\right)^n, \qquad n \ge \frac{\log(A_{RF}/V_{\text{allowed}})}{\log(f/f_c)}
$$ {#eq-m15-rf-filter}

With illustrative values, 10 V of RF at 500 kHz reduced to 1 µV with a 500-Hz corner needs order 3 (lab part D). The
filter must come first, because any nonlinearity ahead of it rectifies RF into the signal band:

$$
y = x + \beta x^2, \quad x = A\cos\omega t \;\Longrightarrow\; \overline{y} = \frac{\beta A^2}{2}
$$ {#eq-m15-demod}

The shift follows the RF envelope, so it switches on and off with the ablation and no later filter can remove it.

::: {.demo #m15-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m15-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m15-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m15-d2-rf.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: Butterworth magnitude responses, @eq-m15-rf-filter; RF frequency range from @berjano2006. Tested against
  `epml.safety`.
- Parameters: corner, RF amplitude at the input and allowed residual are adjustable illustrative choices.
- What it ignores: component tolerances, parasitic capacitance that bypasses the filter at RF, the protection network's
  own response, and demodulation (@eq-m15-demod).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Protect inputs against the procedure's own energy: clamps for pulses, filters for RF.
- Filter RF before anything nonlinear.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** An EP procedure connects several devices to one patient: a recording system, a mapping
system, a stimulator and an ablation generator, often through catheters in the heart. In patients at defibrillator
testing, 60-Hz currents below the then-current 50 µA single-fault standard caused continuous ventricular capture and
hypotension that the ECG did not reveal, and the authors proposed a lower limit for currents lasting 5 seconds or more
[@swerdlow1999]. Fluid-filled lines can carry leakage to a central catheter [@jonsson2005]. Combinations of equipment
can create risks that no single device has [@burgess2019].

**What the evidence is.** A clinical threshold study in 40 patients [@swerdlow1999], a bench study [@jonsson2005] and a
review [@burgess2019]. The safety standards themselves are not reproduced here.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **What is the total leakage with every device connected?** (@eq-m15-leakage)
- **Which connections reach the heart directly?** (@eq-m15-density)
- **Is every input rated for defibrillation and for the ablation energy in use?** (@eq-m15-defib, @eq-m15-rf-filter)

## How experts think

When a design or a setup connects to the heart, ask:

1. **Where can current flow to the patient, in normal use and with one fault?** (@eq-m15-leakage)
2. **What is the total with every connected device?** (@eq-m15-leakage)
3. **Which paths are intracardiac, and how small are their electrodes?** (@eq-m15-density)
4. **What energy will the procedure itself put on the inputs?** (@eq-m15-defib, @eq-m15-rf-filter)
5. **Is every nonlinearity behind the filter?** (@eq-m15-demod)

One sentence to keep: **near the heart, microamperes matter; every path and every device counts.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Capacitive leakage (@eq-m15-leakage) | $2\pi f C V$; in-phase sum; $C_{\max} = I_{\lim}/(2\pi f V)$ |
| Current density (@eq-m15-density) | $I/(2\pi r^2)$; concentration $A/(2\pi a^2)$ |
| Defibrillation protection (@eq-m15-defib) | $(V_{in} - V_c)/R$; $E_R = (V_{in} - V_c)^2T/R$ |
| RF filtering (@eq-m15-rf-filter) | $\approx (f_c/f)^n$; $n \ge \log(A/V_{\text{allowed}})/\log(f/f_c)$ |
| Demodulation (@eq-m15-demod) | $\beta A^2/2$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| 60-Hz thresholds 20, 32 and 49 µA; 50 µA standard; 22% and 12% at or below it | @swerdlow1999 |
| CF limit of 50 µA used in a bench test | @jonsson2005 |
| RF ablation at 300 kHz to 1 MHz | @berjano2006 |
| Capacitances, mains voltages, radii, areas, pulse values, RF amplitudes, β | illustrative |
| Leakage currents, maximum capacitances, filter orders, energies | our own code |

## Practice questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In your answer, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Why is a catheter connection more dangerous than a skin electrode at the same current?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The current enters the heart through a small electrode, so its density there is $I/(2\pi a^2)$ instead of being
spread over the body (@eq-m15-density).

</details>

**Q2. What did the 1999 clinical threshold study find?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In 40 patients, 60-Hz current through a ventricular catheter caused intermittent capture from 20 µA, continuous capture
from 32 µA and fibrillation from 49 µA; continuous capture caused hypotension without ECG evidence [@swerdlow1999].

</details>

**Q3. How does isolation capacitance create leakage, and how would you budget it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It passes $2\pi f C V$ at mains frequency; sum the worst case over every device on the patient and keep it under the
limit (@eq-m15-leakage).

</details>

**Q4. Why can two compliant devices together be a problem?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Their leakages can add in phase through the same patient (@eq-m15-leakage) [@burgess2019].

</details>

**Q5. A barrier has 200 pF. Leakage at 230 V, 50 Hz?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About 14.5 µA (@eq-m15-leakage).

</details>

**Q6. How does a series-resistor-and-clamp network protect an input during defibrillation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The clamp limits the voltage at the amplifier; the resistor limits the current to $(V_{in} - V_c)/R$ and absorbs
$(V_{in} - V_c)^2T/R$ (@eq-m15-defib).

</details>

**Q7. What is the trade-off in choosing the series resistor?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Larger $R$ means less current, energy and diversion, but more thermal noise (m14) and a lower corner with the input
capacitance (@eq-m15-defib).

</details>

**Q8. Why must RF be filtered before the first active stage?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Any nonlinearity rectifies RF into a baseband shift $\beta A^2/2$ that follows the ablation on and off, and no later
filter can remove it (@eq-m15-demod).

</details>

**Q9. How do you size an RF filter?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

From the RF amplitude at the input, the allowed residual, the RF frequency and the corner:
$n \ge \log(A/V_{\text{allowed}})/\log(f/f_c)$ (@eq-m15-rf-filter).

</details>

**Q10. What does "CF" mean for an applied part?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Cardiac floating: the IEC 60601-1 class of applied part for direct cardiac connection. A bench study argued that
dialysis machines used with central catheters should be classed CF rather than B [@jonsson2005].

</details>

**Q11. Can fluid lines carry leakage?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Yes: in a bench test, dialysis blood lines carried leakage above the CF limit to a central catheter's tip in several
conditions [@jonsson2005].

</details>

**Q12. Leakage at 20 µA was invisible on the ECG yet caused capture. What does that teach a system designer?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

That safety cannot rely on a clinician noticing; it must be designed in through isolation, budgets and testing
[@swerdlow1999].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. Doubling the isolation capacitance does what to the leakage?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Doubles it (@eq-m15-leakage).

</details>

**S2. Three devices each leak 8 µA in phase. Total?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

24 µA (@eq-m15-leakage).

</details>

**S3. Electrode radius halves, same current. Density at its surface?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Four times higher (@eq-m15-density).

</details>

**S4. 210 V at an input, 10 V clamp, 10 kΩ. Current?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

20 mA (@eq-m15-defib).

</details>

**S5. A first-order low-pass at 500 Hz. Attenuation at 500 kHz?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 1000-fold, 60 dB (@eq-m15-rf-filter).

</details>

**S6. RF amplitude doubles before a square-law nonlinearity. Baseband shift?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Four times larger (@eq-m15-demod).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Capture without an ECG sign.** Swerdlow and colleagues' recordings of arterial pressure during 60-Hz current
  [@swerdlow1999]. This module: microshock and current density.
- **Leakage through fluid lines.** Jonsson and colleagues' measurements on dialysis blood lines [@jonsson2005]. This
  module: leakage through isolation.
